voiceInstructions: Warm, precise American English mathematics teacher. Read set membership, intervals and compositions carefully. Use natural pauses after questions. Do not omit the final sentence or add words absent from the script.
title: Sets, relations and functions: classification, composition and inverses

sources.title: NCERT Mathematics XII: Relations and Functions

chapters.title: Represent sets and count their subsets
points: Sets ignore order and repetition.
The empty set differs from a set containing the empty set.
Membership and subset statements are different.
chapters.script: A set is a well defined collection of distinct objects. We may list its members or describe them by a rule. The set of positive even integers less than eight is two, four, six. Reordering that list or repeating four does not change the set. Membership asks whether one object is a member; a subset statement asks whether every member of one set belongs to another. The empty set has no members and is a subset of every set. A set containing the empty set has one member, so it is different from the empty set itself. The power set collects all subsets. If A has three distinct elements, decide independently whether to include each element. Two choices at each of three positions give eight subsets. The empty set and A itself are included. A proper subset must differ from A, so seven of those eight are proper. Do not subtract the empty set merely because it looks unusual. For the empty set, its power set has one member, namely the empty set. In set builder notation, always specify the underlying number system and restrictions. The equation x squared equals one selects two real numbers, while the condition x is a positive real number selects only the positive solution.

chapters.title: Use set algebra with a stated universal set
chapters.formula: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ; (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ
points: Complement depends on the universal set.
Difference A∖B equals A∩Bᶜ.
Distribute intersection over union and union over intersection.
chapters.script: Fix the universal set before taking a complement. Let U contain the integers one through six, A contain one, two, three, and B contain three, four. The union contains one, two, three, four; the intersection contains only three. The complement of A contains four, five, six. The difference A minus B contains one, two, whereas B minus A contains four. Set difference is therefore not commutative. De Morgan's laws explain how a complement crosses a union or intersection. Not belonging to either A or B means belonging to both complements, so the complement of their union is the intersection of their complements. Not belonging to their intersection means failing at least one membership condition, so it gives the union of complements. Intersection distributes over union, and union distributes over intersection. You can check a proposed identity by following one arbitrary element and its membership conditions. For example, membership in A intersect B union C means membership in A and membership in at least one of B or C. This becomes the union of A intersect B and A intersect C. Keep brackets clear: changing them can change the set being described.

chapters.title: Count unions without double counting
points: Pairwise intersections include triple membership.
Exactly one and at least one are different counts.
Subtract the union from the universal total for neither.
chapters.script: Counting union members requires correcting repeated counts. Suppose a group has forty students, twenty four in A, nineteen in B, and eight in both. Adding twenty four and nineteen counts those eight students twice. Subtract them once to obtain thirty five in at least one set, leaving five in neither. Exactly one set contains twenty four plus nineteen minus twice eight, giving twenty seven. With three sets, add the three sizes, subtract all three pairwise intersection sizes, then add the triple intersection once. Why add it back? A student in all three was counted three times initially and subtracted three times, so needs one final count. For sizes twenty, eighteen, fifteen, pairwise intersection sizes eight, seven, six, and triple size three, the union has thirty five members. The number in exactly two sets is the sum of the pairwise sizes minus three times the triple size, giving twelve. Pairwise intersection counts ordinarily include students in the third set unless the wording explicitly says otherwise. Draw disjoint regions starting at the triple intersection when the data feel confusing. Finally, verify that every derived region is nonnegative and that the union does not exceed the supplied group size.

chapters.title: Distinguish relation properties using ordered pairs
chapters.formula: R ⊆ A×A; reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive are separate tests
points: Reflexive requires every diagonal pair.
Symmetric reverses each related pair.
Antisymmetric allows both directions only for equal elements.
chapters.script: A binary relation from A to B is a subset of the Cartesian product A cross B. Each member is an ordered pair, so reversing its entries need not preserve membership. For a relation on A, reflexivity requires every pair a, a. Symmetry says that whenever a, b belongs, b, a also belongs. Antisymmetry says that if both a, b and b, a belong, then a must equal b. This is not simply the opposite of symmetry: the identity relation is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Transitivity requires a, c whenever a, b and b, c belong. Consider the less than or equal relation on real numbers. It is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, but not symmetric. The relation of having the same absolute value is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. To disprove a property, one counterexample is enough. To establish it for an infinite set, use an argument covering arbitrary elements rather than checking only a few examples. The empty relation on a nonempty set is not reflexive, while symmetry and transitivity hold because no pairs trigger a failure. Always state the underlying set: changing it can change the truth of a property.

chapters.title: Build equivalence classes from an equivalence relation
chapters.formula: aRb ⇔ a−b is divisible by 3; classes [0], [1], [2]
points: Equivalence means reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Classes either coincide or are disjoint.
The classes partition the original set.
chapters.script: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. These three conditions make its equivalence classes divide the underlying set into disjoint groups. On the integers, define a related to b when a minus b is divisible by three. Reflexivity follows because a minus a is zero, a multiple of three. If a minus b is divisible by three, its negative b minus a is too, establishing symmetry. If a minus b and b minus c are divisible by three, their sum a minus c is divisible by three, establishing transitivity. Integers fall into three classes according to remainder zero, one or two after division by three. Negative integers belong too: negative one is in the same class as two because their difference is negative three. Every integer belongs to exactly one class, and two classes sharing a member must be the same class. This is the partition property. Conversely, a partition defines an equivalence relation by declaring two elements related when they lie in the same block. Do not use a merely symmetric relation as an equivalence relation without checking transitivity and reflexivity. For example, being unequal is symmetric on the integers but fails reflexivity and also fails transitivity.
board: −1 and 2 lie in the same class

chapters.title: Keep domain, codomain and range distinct
points: Every domain input needs exactly one output.
A codomain is specified; range is actually reached.
Real square roots and zero denominators restrict the domain.
chapters.script: A function from A to B assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A. Multiple inputs may share an output, but one input cannot have two different outputs. The domain is A, the codomain is B, and the range is the collection of outputs actually reached. For the square function from the reals to the reals, negative outputs are never reached, so the range is the nonnegative reals and is smaller than the codomain. If an algebraic formula is supplied without a domain, first identify the real inputs where the formula is defined. For the square root of x minus one divided by x minus three, the square root requires x at least one, and the denominator excludes three. Combine the conditions rather than treating either as sufficient. The domain is from one inclusive to three exclusive, together with numbers greater than three. Cancelling a factor does not automatically restore an excluded input from the original expression. For example, x squared minus one divided by x minus one agrees with x plus one only when x is not one. Writing the original domain prevents an algebraic simplification from silently defining a different function.

chapters.title: Classify injective, onto, into and bijective functions
chapters.formula: Injective: f(a)=f(b) ⇒ a=b; onto: range = codomain
points: One-one concerns repeated outputs from different inputs.
Onto depends on the specified codomain.
Bijective means both injective and onto.
chapters.script: A function is injective, or one to one, when equal outputs imply equal inputs. It is onto, or surjective, when every member of its codomain is reached. A function whose range is a proper subset of its codomain is often called into. These conditions answer different questions. The square function from the reals to the reals is neither injective nor onto: one and negative one share an output, and negative numbers are missed. Keep the real domain but change the codomain to the nonnegative reals. It becomes onto but remains noninjective. Restrict both domain and codomain to the nonnegative reals. It is now injective and onto, hence bijective. An affine function two x plus three from the reals to the reals is bijective: equal outputs give equal inputs, and any target y has input y minus three divided by two. A constant function on a domain with at least two elements is not injective, but it is onto a codomain containing only its constant value. State the sets every time; a formula alone does not settle the classification. Use a counterexample to refute injectivity and solve for a preimage to establish surjectivity.
board: x²: ℝ→ℝ is neither one-one nor onto

chapters.title: Count functions, injections and finite bijections
chapters.formula: |A|=m, |B|=n: functions nᵐ; injections n!/(n−m)! when m≤n
points: Each input independently chooses an output for general functions.
Injective choices cannot reuse an output.
Equal finite sizes make injectivity and surjectivity equivalent.
chapters.script: For a finite domain containing m elements and a finite codomain containing n elements, each input can independently choose any of n outputs. This gives n to the power m functions. With a three element domain and a two element codomain, there are eight functions. Exactly two are constant, and the other six hit both target elements, so there are six onto functions in this particular case. There are no injections because three distinct inputs cannot have distinct outputs in only two target positions. Reverse the sizes: a two element domain and three element codomain give nine functions and six injections, but no surjections. An injection uses three choices for the first output and two for the second. In general, for m no greater than n, the injection count is n factorial divided by n minus m factorial. If m exceeds n, it is zero. A bijection between two finite sets of the same size n is a permutation of the targets, giving n factorial choices. For equal finite sizes, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent, but this shortcut is not a general rule for infinite sets. Keep the finite hypothesis attached to the counting argument.

chapters.title: Compose functions in the correct order and domain
points: The inner function acts first.
Composition is not generally commutative.
Check restrictions before simplifying the composite.
chapters.script: Composition feeds one function's output into another. In f composed with g, the inner function g acts first. Let f of x equal two x plus one and g of x equal x squared. Then f of g of x is two x squared plus one, whereas g of f of x is the square of two x plus one. These functions differ, so order matters. A composite requires x in the domain of g and g of x in the domain of f. Consider f of u equal one divided by u minus one, and g of x equal the square root of x. The composite is one divided by the square root of x minus one. The inner function requires x at least zero, while the outer denominator excludes square root of x equal to one, so exclude x equal to one. Its domain is the nonnegative reals with one removed. Composition is associative when all the stated maps are compatible, even though it is not commutative. Thus f composed with g composed with h can be bracketed in either association without reversing their order. Before cancelling an expression or rearranging a composition, write the original input conditions so no forbidden point is accidentally restored.

chapters.title: Find inverses by choosing a bijective domain
chapters.formula: f⁻¹∘f = I_A; f∘f⁻¹ = I_B for a bijection f:A→B
points: An inverse function reverses input and output roles.
f⁻¹ does not mean the reciprocal 1/f.
A domain restriction can make a noninjective formula invertible.
chapters.script: An inverse function undoes a bijection. If f maps A bijectively onto B, its inverse maps B back to A. Composing the inverse after f gives the identity on A, and composing f after its inverse gives the identity on B. The notation f inverse is not a reciprocal. For f of x equal two x plus three on the reals, solve y equals two x plus three for x. This gives x equal to y minus three divided by two, so the inverse takes an input y to that value. Verify both compositions, not just a symbolic swap. The square function on all reals has no inverse function because positive and negative inputs can share an output. Restrict the original domain to the nonnegative reals and take the nonnegative reals as codomain. Then its inverse is the nonnegative square root. The alternative negative half line produces a different inverse branch. For f of x equal x squared minus four on x at least zero, the codomain must be the interval starting at negative four for a bijection. Its inverse is square root of y plus four. Domain and codomain restrictions therefore determine which inverse is valid.
board: x² on ℝ has no inverse function

quiz.question: How many subsets does {a, b, c} have?
quiz.explanation: Each of the three distinct elements is either included or excluded, so there are 2³ = 8 subsets, including the empty and full sets.

quiz.question: If |A| = 12, |B| = 9 and |A ∩ B| = 4, what is |A ∪ B|?
quiz.explanation: 12 + 9 counts the four shared elements twice. Subtract 4 once: 17.

quiz.question: Which relation is a function with domain {1, 2}?
quiz.explanation: Both domain elements receive exactly one output. The same output for two different inputs is allowed.

quiz.question: What is the natural real domain of 1/sqrt(x - 4)?
quiz.explanation: The radicand must be non-negative, but the square root is also a denominator and cannot be zero. Together these require x - 4 > 0.

quiz.question: If f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = 2x, what is f(g(2))?
quiz.explanation: Apply g first: g(2) = 4. Then f(4) = 7. The value 10 comes from reversing the order.

quiz.question: How many proper subsets does a set of 4 distinct elements have?
quiz.explanation: There are 2⁴=16 subsets, including the whole set. Remove only the whole set to obtain 15 proper subsets; the empty set remains included.

quiz.question: For U={1,2,3,4,5,6}, A={1,2,3}, B={3,4}, A∖B is:
quiz.explanation: A∖B contains members of A that do not belong to B. Remove the shared element 3 from A, leaving the set {1,2}.

quiz.question: The complement of A∪B, relative to a fixed U, is:
quiz.explanation: De Morgan’s law says an element is outside the union exactly when it is outside both sets, giving the intersection of the two complements.

quiz.question: In a group of 40, |A|=24, |B|=19 and |A∩B|=8. How many are in neither?
quiz.explanation: The union has 24+19−8=35 members. Subtract that from the universal total 40 to obtain 5 students in neither set.

quiz.question: For three sets of sizes 20,18,15, pairwise intersections 8,7,6 and triple intersection 3, the union size is:
quiz.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives 20+18+15−8−7−6+3=35. Pairwise intersections already include the triple intersection.

quiz.question: Which property requires that (a,b) and (b,a) in R imply a=b?
quiz.explanation: Antisymmetry allows a pair and its reverse simultaneously only when their entries coincide. It is different from the property called symmetry.

quiz.question: An equivalence relation must be:
quiz.explanation: All three properties are required. Together they ensure equivalence classes form disjoint blocks whose union is the underlying set.

quiz.question: On ℤ, aRb means 3 divides a−b. Which pair lies in one equivalence class?
quiz.explanation: The difference −1−2 is −3, a multiple of 3. The two integers therefore have the same remainder class modulo 3.

quiz.question: The real domain of √(x−1)/(x−3) is:
quiz.explanation: The square root requires x≥1 and the denominator requires x≠3. Intersecting the conditions gives the stated two intervals.

quiz.question: The function f:ℝ→[0,∞), f(x)=x², is:
quiz.explanation: Every nonnegative target has a real square root, so the map is onto. Inputs 1 and −1 have the same output, so it is not injective.

quiz.question: Which square-function specification is bijective?
quiz.explanation: Restricting to nonnegative inputs makes squaring injective, and every nonnegative target is reached. Both conditions for bijection hold.

quiz.question: How many functions map a 3-element set onto a 2-element set?
quiz.explanation: There are 2³=8 functions in total. Exactly two are constant and fail to hit both targets; the remaining 6 are onto.

quiz.question: How many injections map a 2-element set into a 3-element set?
quiz.explanation: The first input has three possible outputs and the second must use one of the other two. Thus the injection count is 3×2=6.

quiz.question: For f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x², (f∘g)(x) is:
quiz.explanation: Apply g first to obtain x², then apply f. The result is 2x²+1; reversing the order would give (2x+1)².

quiz.question: The domain of 1/(√x−1) over the reals is:
quiz.explanation: The square root requires x≥0 and the denominator vanishes at x=1. Zero is permitted, but one must be excluded.

quiz.question: For f:[0,∞)→[−4,∞), f(x)=x²−4, the inverse is:
quiz.explanation: The original nonnegative domain chooses the positive square-root branch. Solving y=x²−4 gives x=√(y+4) for y≥−4.
